deed: רב סעדיה גאון תרגם את התורה לערבית ועיצב את סידור התפילה
title: Saadia Gaon translated the Torah into Arabic and composed a prayer book, and his translation spread among the Jewish communities of the East

trailer.text: According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, he was born in Egypt; according to Eliezer Schlossberg, he moved from there to Babylonia, the center of Jewish creativity in those days.
He translated the Torah into Arabic in Hebrew letters, in a book called "Tafsir".
The translation spread quickly among the Jewish communities of the Near East, North Africa and Muslim Spain.

paragraphs.text: According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, Saadia was born in Dilaẓ, in Upper Egypt.
In the book Sefer ha-Galui, he himself traced his lineage to the family of Shelah, the son of Judah.
According to Eliezer Schlossberg, he left Egypt for unknown reasons and turned to Babylonia.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, in 913, in his twentieth year, Saadia completed his first great work, a Hebrew dictionary which he called "Egron".
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, this dictionary became the foundation of Hebrew lexicography.
According to the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Saadia Gaon was probably born in 882 in Ḍilaẓ, a village in the Fayyūm district in Egypt.
According to Al HaTorah, in the summer of 921 Ben Meir planned to declare that the months of Marheshvan and Kislev would have 29 days, contrary to the calendar rules of the Babylonian Geonim.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, this ordinance endangered the unity of Judaism, and when Saadia learned of it he immediately sent Ben Meir a warning.
According to the Al HaTorah website, R. Saadia took part in a campaign to convince all Jews, including those in the Land of Israel, to follow the calendar of the Babylonian Geonim.
In 928 the Exilarch David ben Zakkai appointed Saadia Gaon of the Sura Academy.
According to Vollandt, the academy had by then already moved to Baghdad, the political centre of the Abbasid caliphate.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, the ancient academy, founded by Rab, then entered a new period of flourishing.
According to Al HaTorah, until his time the Geonim wrote mainly responsa, and Saadia Gaon changed the role of the Gaon by composing numerous works in many genres.
In the introduction to his translations, Saadia Gaon wrote that he had long wished that a translation of the Torah made by his own hands would be found among the people of his faith.
He was not the first to translate the Bible into Arabic, and his writings allude to translation traditions that preceded him.
According to Schlossberg, Arabic translations from before his time are known, and fragments of them have been published in recent years.
The translation was produced in the first third of the tenth century, and was initially part of a commentary.
According to Sefaria, the book "Tafsir", the translation of the Torah into Arabic in Hebrew letters, was composed approximately between 918 and 942.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, the prayer book contains the entire order for weekdays, Sabbaths and festivals, with explanations in Arabic.
According to Al HaTorah, it was a popular prayer book, and it contains short halakhic discussions of the laws of prayer and the holidays.
Saadia Gaon's translation spread quickly among the Jewish communities of the Near East, North Africa and Muslim Spain.
According to Vollandt, it also spread quickly beyond these communities, and among Jews it reached the status of the standard, almost canonical, Arabic version of the Bible.
According to Vollandt, the material evidence for the Tafsir includes hundreds of full manuscripts.
According to him, the manuscript in St. Petersburg, copied about sixty years after the Gaon's death, preserves the translation in the most precise language.
According to Vollandt, the Torah translation was also preserved in many Christian manuscripts in Arabic letters, which were used by Monophysite communities.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, the translation of the Pentateuch was printed in the Polyglot Bibles of Constantinople (1546), Paris (1645) and London (1657).

According to Al HaTorah, Saadia Gaon's writings were written in Arabic in Hebrew letters, in an orthographic system that he may have invented, and it became the standard for Jews who wrote Arabic for several centuries.
According to Vollandt, the language and transcription system of the translation became exemplary and authoritative.
According to Tobi, in the second edition of the "Egron" and of "Sefer ha-Galui" Saadia added an Arabic section, and thus gave legitimacy to the use of Arabic in Jewish poetry and liturgy.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, the translation presented the Scriptures even to the unlearned in a rational form, which aimed at the greatest possible clarity and consistency.
According to the same encyclopedia, Saadia's Bible translation served for centuries as an important factor in bringing Arabic culture into the Jewish spirit.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, what moved Saadia to compose the book Ha-Emunot ve-ha-De'ot was his grief at the confusion concerning matters of religion among his contemporaries.
According to the same encyclopedia, the book was completed in 933, and it is the first systematic presentation and philosophical foundation of the dogmas of Judaism.
According to Al HaTorah, the book was among the most widely read and influential rabbinic books of philosophy of the Middle Ages.

According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, Karaism, which had begun to take root about one hundred and fifty years earlier, threatened, according to Saadia, to overcome Rabbinic Judaism, whose Babylonian academies had begun to lose their standing.
According to the same encyclopedia, Saadia, a man of broad knowledge and secular learning, fought the enemies of Jewish tradition.
According to Vollandt, he devoted considerable energy to polemics against the Karaites and other non-Rabbanite movements.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, Saadia's Hebrew grammar is the oldest one known.

According to the same encyclopedia, the historical importance of Saadia himself is due primarily to his establishment of a new school of Biblical exegesis, characterized by a rational investigation of the contents of the Bible.
The Jewish Encyclopedia states that after Philo, Saadia was the first great writer in post-Biblical Judaism.

stations.title: The conflict with the Exilarch, and what was said against him

paragraphs.text: In a matter concerning a will, Saadia refused to sign a ruling of the Exilarch which he considered unjust.
After the exilarch's son threatened the gaon with violence to make him sign, and the gaon's servant treated him roughly, open war broke out between the exilarch and the gaon.
According to Al HaTorah, because of the dispute with the Exilarch David ben Zakkai, Saadia Gaon was removed from his post.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, the seven years Saadia spent in Baghdad, far from the gaonate, did not interrupt his literary activity.
According to the same encyclopedia, he was reinstated in his office, but held it for only five years.
He died in 942, according to the Jewish Encyclopedia at the age of fifty.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, his enemies alluded to the lowly occupation of his father, and even described his father as a non-Jew.
According to the same encyclopedia, they spread malicious stories about his origin, and these stories probably had no basis.

According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, four years after 933, that is, in 937, the rivals were reconciled and Saadia Gaon was reinstated in the gaonate, which he held for only five years.

According to the Al HaTorah website, Ibn Ezra, in his introduction to his Torah commentary, was displeased that R. Saadia Gaon included in his long commentary other views according to the scholars of the sciences, for example in the commentary on Yehi me'orot (Let there be lights).
